extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of logic, philosophy of language, and semantics
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition and taxonomy of kinds of names (concrete/abstract, connotative/non-connotative, relative/absolute, etc.) and the implications of these distinctions for meaning and proper use of language. Useful for analyzing, defining, and improving precision in philosophical and logical discourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concrete vs. Abstract names
rubrics_metrics.description: By 'abstract' mean the opposite of 'concrete'; an abstract name is the name of an attribute, a concrete name is the name of an object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and clarification: 'whiteness' is an abstract name (the color), 'white' is used as a concrete name (predicated of objects: snow is white). Historical note: the older (schoolmen) usage restricted 'abstract' to names of attributes; modern usage often misapplies it to all general names. Use the term 'concrete' for object-names and 'abstract' for attribute-names to avoid confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract names: general vs singular
rubrics_metrics.description: Some abstract names are general (names of a class of attributes) while others designate a single, determinate attribute and may be neither general nor individual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'color' and 'whiteness' (in respect of different shades) can be general; 'visibleness' or 'milk-whiteness' designate one determinate attribute and may be treated as neither general nor individual. When classifying, consider whether the abstract term covers a plurality of attribute-instances or a single determinate attribute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connotative vs. Non-connotative (absolute) names
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-connotative terms signify a subject only or an attribute only; connotative terms denote a subject and imply (connote) an attribute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: proper names like 'John' or 'London' are non-connotative; 'white' is connotative because it denotes white things and implies the attribute 'whiteness'. All concrete general names are connotative. Recognize that connotation is what carries informative meaning in many names; distinguishing denotation from connotation is crucial to analyzing meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Denotation vs. Connotation: meaning resides in connotation
rubrics_metrics.description: When names convey information the meaning resides not in what they denote (the objects named) but in what they connote (the attributes implied).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proper names function mainly as marks of identity and connote nothing (thus have, strictly speaking, no signification). Connotative names, by contrast, provide new information by implying attributes (e.g., 'built of marble' conveys the attribute). Use this distinction to evaluate how much semantic content a name actually carries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fix the connotation of frequently used general concrete names
rubrics_metrics.description: To remedy vagueness in language, give every general concrete name that is frequently predicated a definite and fixed connotation so it is clear what attributes are meant to be predicated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definitions of connotative names are attempts to declare or analyze connotation. The objective is to fix connotation with minimal disruption to the set of objects the name habitually denotes and with minimal falsification of commonly received propositions. This is a normative guideline for philosophers and scientific writers to promote precision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid using connotative terms without ascertained connotation
rubrics_metrics.description: Using connotative terms without a distinctly ascertained connotation leads to lax habits of thought and vague discourse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text warns of the common human tendency to generalize words by superficial similarity, causing words to lose coherent connotation. This is an anti-pattern: avoid relying solely on examples of denotation to infer meaning; instead, analyze and, where needed, define the connotation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper names vs. connotative individual names
rubrics_metrics.description: Proper names denote individuals and do not indicate attributes (they are 'unmeaning marks'), but some individual names can be connotative when an attribute uniquely identifies a single object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Paul' or 'Caesar' are proper names (no connotation). Phrases like 'the only son of John Stiles' or 'the present prime minister of England' are individual names that connote attributes (uniqueness, relation to an event, or temporal limitation). Distinguish between mere labels and individually identifying descriptive names.

rubrics_metrics.name: Positive vs. Negative names (including privative)
rubrics_metrics.description: Names divide into positive (e.g., 'man', 'good') and negative (e.g., 'not-man'). Negative concrete names denote all things except those denoted by the positive name and connote absence of an attribute. Privative names combine absence of an expected attribute with presence of other attributes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that form and reality can diverge: words with negative form (unpleasant) may connote a positive attribute, and positive-form words (idle) may express mere absence. Privative example: 'blind' implies absence of sight plus expectation that the class normally has sight; treat privatives as connoting both absence and other present attributes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative vs. Non-relative (relative and correlative) names
rubrics_metrics.description: Relative names (father/son, ruler/subject, cause/effect) are given in pairs and, over and above the object they denote, imply the existence of another object with which the relation holds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The attribute connoted by a relative name is a relation grounded in a series of events (fundamentum relationis). When analyzing relative terms, account for the correlative counterpart and the underlying fact or series of events they both express (e.g., 'A is father of B' and 'B is son of A' assert the same fact in different modes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Univocal, Aequivocal, and Analogical (metaphorical) use of names
rubrics_metrics.description: A name is univocal when applied in the same sense to all things it predicates of; aequivocal/ambiguous when predicated in different senses; analogical when predicated in similar but not identical senses (metaphor).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ambiguous/equivocal words are effectively different words sharing a sound; analogical/metaphorical uses derive a secondary sense from a primary one (e.g., 'brilliant' for light and achievement). Beware fallacious reasoning that treats metaphorical expressions as if literal (arguing from a metaphor as if it were literal).

rubrics_metrics.name: Vagueness in connotation can be tolerable but must be guarded
rubrics_metrics.description: Partial uncertainty in connotation (vagueness about how far a term applies) can exist without practical harm under certain classification conditions, but requires strict precautions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'man' has unsettled connotation concerning required external form or minimal rationality. In natural history and classification, some vagueness may be preferable to overprecision. Nonetheless, guard vagueness by clear contextual use, explicit definitions where precision is needed, and awareness of when vagueness might mislead.
